sources: Adolph, Cole, Komati, Garciaguirre, Badaly, Lingeman, Chan and Sotsky. How do you learn to walk? Thousands of steps and dozens of falls per day. Psychological Science 23(11):1387-1394 (2012).
Hoch, O'Grady and Adolph. It's the journey not the destination: locomotor exploration in infants. Developmental Science (2019). 2,400 to 4,200 steps per hour, the same magnitude.

slides.lead: A toddler takes 2,368 steps an hour. And falls 17 times.
slides.sub: Nobody scheduled it. Nobody drilled it. 151 infants, filmed at ordinary play.

figure.label: falls per hour, ages 12 to 19 months, during free play

slides.head: The setup
slides.body:
For a century, walking was studied by coaxing infants down a straight, flat path.

In 2012 Karen Adolph's lab at NYU filmed 151 infants aged 12 to 19 months during ordinary free play, then coded every step and every fall from video, frame by frame.

slides.head: One hour of play
slides.body: Per hour, and the infants were only in motion a third of the time. Nearly half of all walking bouts were one to three steps long.

slides.head: So why give up crawling?
slides.body:
New walkers fell almost twice as often per hour as expert crawlers, yet they were the ones who abandoned crawling.

Because walking took them three times as far. Per distance covered, the fall rate was the same. Falling is not the price of walking. It is the price of moving.

slides.head: The catch, and the point
slides.body:
One lab, one culture, one age window, and later work puts the step count even higher.

The point stands: a practice regimen this large and this varied came out of play. When a new walker falls, gets up and staggers off again, that is what you are watching.
